title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors and Diagonalisation
objectives: Find eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix via the characteristic polynomial and verify eigenvectors
Verify and construct a diagonalisation A = PDP^{-1} and explain when it exists
Compute matrix powers using the diagonal form
Explain how the eigendecomposition of a covariance matrix produces principal components and variance shares
motivation: An eigendirection of a real matrix is a nonzero line mapped to itself: it can be stretched, reversed or collapsed. Not every real matrix has a real eigenvector; a90-degree planar rotation has none. Real symmetric covariance matrices do have an orthonormal eigenbasis, which makes their principal-component interpretation especially useful. Uncorrelated principal components are not automatically statistically independent.

blocks.md: Apply a matrix to a typical vector and two things happen: it is stretched *and* rotated. An **eigenvector** of $A$ is the exception, a nonzero vector $v$ satisfying the algebraic relation below: $Av = \lambda v$ for some scalar $\lambda$, the **eigenvalue**. The eigenvalue records the stretch factor: $\lambda = 2$ doubles the length, $\lambda = 0.5$ halves it, $\lambda = 0$ collapses the vector to the origin (and note: $\lambda = 0$ in the spectrum means $\det(A) = 0$ - singular). A negative real eigenvalue reverses the arrow, and a zero eigenvalue maps it to zero, where direction is undefined. Eigenvectors are defined only up to nonzero scale: $(1, -2)$ and $(2, -4)$ describe the same eigendirection, which is why libraries return arbitrary normalisations.

The field matters: a90-degree real rotation has characteristic polynomial lambda^2+1 and eigenvalues+i,-i over the complex numbers, but no real eigendirection. A real symmetric matrix instead has real eigenvalues and can use a real orthonormal basis. Distinguish a real diagonalisation from a complex one before asserting existence.

blocks.caption: A nonzero null vector exists exactly when A-lambda*I is singular. The determinant condition establishes existence, not that every chosen v is an eigenvector.

blocks.title: Worked example: full eigendecomposition of a 2x2
items: Factor: $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 10 = (\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 5)$, so the eigenvalues are $\lambda = 2$ and $\lambda = 5$.

blocks.caption: For A=[[4,1],[2,3]],(1,1) is scaled by5 and(1,-2) by2. Both eigendirections stay on their own lines; it is false that every other direction than(1,1) bends away. This static image has no draggable test-point control.

blocks.md: Collect the eigenvectors as columns of a matrix $P$ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of a matrix $D$. Then $AP = PD$ says exactly what the worked example verified: $A$ acting on each eigenvector just scales it. If $P$ is invertible (true when you found $n$ independent eigenvectors), this rearranges to the **diagonalisation** $A = P D P^{-1}$: change into eigen-coordinates ($P^{-1}$), scale each axis independently ($D$), change back ($P$). Diagonalisation turns hard matrix questions into easy diagonal ones, most importantly powers:

blocks.tex: A^k = (P D P^{-1})^k = P \, D^k \, P^{-1}, \qquad D^k = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1^k & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2^k \end{pmatrix}
blocks.caption: Repeated application is just repeated scaling along each eigendirection.

blocks.md: Two useful cross-checks: eigenvalues always sum to the **trace** ($\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = a + d$) and multiply to the **determinant** ($\lambda_1 \lambda_2 = \det A$). In the example: $2 + 5 = 7 = 4 + 3$ ✓ and $2 \times 5 = 10 = 12 - 2$ ✓. If a matrix has fewer than $n$ independent eigenvectors it is **defective** and cannot be diagonalised (symmetric matrices never have this problem, and their eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are automatically orthogonal).

blocks.text: Why quants care: PCA in one paragraph

blocks.md: A real covariance matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite and has an orthonormal eigenbasis:C=Q*Lambda*Q^T. For a unit eigenvector q_i, the projected return q_i^T*r has variance q_i^T*C*q_i=lambda_i. Without unit normalisation, scaling the weights also scales variance. The leading eigenvector maximises variance among unit-length directions, not among all arbitrarily leveraged portfolios. Principal-component projections are uncorrelated, not generally independent. When trace(C)>0, lambda_i/trace(C) is a share of total coordinate variance, not an individual portfolio contribution-to-risk formula. If all variance is zero the ratio is undefined.

blocks.title: Powers, Markov chains and steady states
blocks.md: For a diagonalizable matrix, powers scale each eigencoordinate by lambda_i^k. A largest-modulus mode dominates only when it is excited and not tied or cancelled; defective matrices can introduce polynomial factors. A finite irreducible aperiodic stochastic matrix converges to a unique stationary distribution under its stated row/column convention. Eigenvalue 1 alone does not ensure convergence: the alternating transition[[0,1],[1,0]] cycles between states. For a column-stochastic matrix the stationary probability column satisfies M*pi=pi, is nonnegative and sums to1.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])            # symmetric example
print(np.linalg.eigvalsh(A))              # [1. 3.] - ascending order
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 2))       # [[5 4]
                                          #  [4 5]]
blocks.caption: For symmetric matrices eigvalsh returns real eigenvalues in ascending order. Check by hand: eigenvalues of [[2,1],[1,2]] are 3 and 1; A^2 = [[5,4],[4,5]].

guidedExercise.prompt: Find the eigenvalues and one eigenvector for each eigenvalue of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, and verify $Av = \lambda v$ for both. (Check: trace $= 2$, det $= -3$.)
hints: For each lambda, solve $(A - \lambda I) v = 0$; one eigenvalue is negative.
For the negative eigenvalue, the output arrow reverses direction but remains on the same line. Verify both coordinates, not only a norm.
guidedExercise.solution: $\det(A - \lambda I) = (1-\lambda)^2 - 4 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1)$, so $\lambda = 3$ and $\lambda = -1$. Cross-check: sum $= 2 = $ trace ✓, product $= -3 = $ det ✓. For $\lambda = 3$: $v = (1, 1)$, since $A(1,1) = (3, 3) = 3(1,1)$ ✓. For $\lambda = -1$: $v = (1, -1)$, since $A(1,-1) = (1-2,\ 2-1) = (-1, 1) = -1 \times (1, -1)$ ✓. Note the two eigenvectors are orthogonal, as they always are for a symmetric matrix.
guidedExercise.successCheck: Eigenpairs are 3 with(1,1) and-1 with(1,-1); both satisfy Av=lambda*v and eigenvalues sum to2, multiply to-3.

independentExercise.prompt: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues 3 and 1, eigenvectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$). (a) Compute $A^2$ directly by matrix multiplication. (b) Use the diagonal form with $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $P^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ to compute $A^3 = P D^3 P^{-1}$ and confirm the direct product $A^3 = A^2 A$.
hints: A^2: four dot products of rows with columns.
In the diagonal form, D^3 = diag(27, 1); carry the 1/2 from P^{-1} through.
Match each column of P to the eigenvalue in the same position in D and check P*P_inverse=I.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 & 2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 \\ 1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 1 & 1 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $A^3 = A^2 A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \cdot 2 + 4 \cdot 1 & 5 \cdot 1 + 4 \cdot 2 \\ 4 \cdot 2 + 5 \cdot 1 & 4 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 14 & 13 \\ 13 & 14 \end{pmatrix}$. (b) $P D^3 = \begin{pmatrix} 27 & 1 \\ 27 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, and $P D^3 P^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 27 + 1 & 27 - 1 \\ 27 - 1 & 27 + 1 \end{pmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 28 & 26 \\ 26 & 28 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 14 & 13 \\ 13 & 14 \end{pmatrix}$ ✓, identical to the direct product, with far less arithmetic.
independentExercise.successCheck: A^2=[[5,4],[4,5]], A^3=[[14,13],[13,14]]; direct multiplication agrees with P*D^3*P_inverse.

commonMistakes: Dividing by zero when solving $(A - \lambda I)v = 0$ - eigenvectors are found by *solving* the singular system, not by inverting.
Forgetting that eigenvectors are only defined up to scale: $(1, -2)$, $(2, -4)$ and $(-0.5, 1)$ are the same eigendirection.
Writing $A = P^{-1} D P$ instead of $A = P D P^{-1}$ - columns of $P$ must be eigenvectors of $A$, in the same order as the diagonal of $D$.
Assuming every matrix is diagonalisable, defective matrices (too few independent eigenvectors) need Jordan/Schur forms instead.
realWorldApplication: Damped PageRank uses a stationary eigenvector of a transition model. In a simple mass-stiffness vibration model, generalised eigenvalues are squared angular frequencies, not raw frequencies. Eigenfaces use eigenvectors of image covariance for a reduced coordinate representation.
quantFinanceApplication: PCA on yield-change covariance can reveal level-like, slope-like and curvature-like modes, but shapes and explained shares depend on the sample, scaling and instruments. Inspect empirical results rather than assuming a fixed variance share or universally parallel leading mode.
summary: An eigenvector is nonzero and satisfies Av=lambda*v. Its line is invariant, though a negative eigenvalue reverses the arrow and zero collapses it; eigenvalues satisfy det(A-lambda*I)=0.
Quick checks: eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
With $n$ independent eigenvectors, $A = PDP^{-1}$ turns powers into $P D^k P^{-1}$ and long-run analysis into reading the dominant eigenvalue.
A covariance matrix has orthonormal eigenvectors and nonnegative eigenvalues. Unit projections have those variances and are uncorrelated; independence needs more assumptions.

quiz.prompt: By definition, $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ when:
quiz.explanation: An eigenvector is nonzero and satisfies Av=lambda*v. Positive lambda stretches without reversing, negative lambda reverses the arrow and zero maps it to the origin. The zero vector is excluded because it would satisfy the equation for every scalar and identify no eigendirection.

quiz.prompt: Without computing eigenvectors: the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ sum to what number? (Hint: trace.)
quiz.explanation: Eigenvalues always sum to the trace: $4 + 3 = 7$. (Indeed $2 + 5 = 7$.) Their product equals the determinant: $2 \times 5 = 10 = 12 - 2$ ✓.

quiz.prompt: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 3 and 1. Which pair of vectors is a pair of eigenvectors?
quiz.explanation: $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}(1,1) = (3,3) = 3(1,1)$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}(1,-1) = (1,-1) = 1(1,-1)$. For a symmetric matrix with distinct eigenvalues, the eigenvectors are orthogonal, and $(1,1) \cdot (1,-1) = 0$ ✓.

quiz.prompt: $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues 3 and $\mu$. What is $\mu$? (Hint: product of eigenvalues = determinant.)
quiz.explanation: The product of eigenvalues is $\det(A) = 1 - 4 = -3$, so $\mu = -3/3 = -1$. (Check via the trace: $3 + (-1) = 2$ ✓.)

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
print(np.linalg.eigvalsh(A))
print(np.linalg.matrix_power(A, 2))
quiz.explanation: eigvalsh returns the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix in ascending order: 1 then 3. The square: $A^2$ entries are $2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 = 5$, $2 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 = 4$, giving [[5, 4], [4, 5]].

quiz.prompt: In PCA on a covariance matrix, what does the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue represent, and what does the eigenvalue itself measure?
quiz.modelAnswer: For unit-normalised weights, the leading eigenvector gives the direction of greatest variance among unit-length directions, and its eigenvalue is that variance. With positive trace, its eigenvalue divided by trace is its share of total variance, not a general portfolio risk contribution.
quiz.explanation: With unit eigenvectors, projected variance is the corresponding eigenvalue. The leading direction maximises variance under a unit-length constraint; lambda/trace is a share only when trace is positive. Scaling the weights changes variance, and uncorrelated projections need not be independent.

quiz.prompt: Which diagonalisation statements are correct over the real numbers?
options: If columns of invertible P are eigenvectors matching diagonal D, A=P*D*P^(-1)
Every real 2-by-2 matrix has two independent real eigenvectors
A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis
quiz.explanation: Diagonalisation needs a complete independent eigenbasis in the chosen field. Real symmetric matrices have one. A real planar rotation can lack real eigenvectors, while the identity has repeated eigenvalues and is already diagonal. Repetition alone neither guarantees nor rules out diagonalisation.

quiz.prompt: A=P*diag(3,1)*P^(-1), with P=[[1,1],[1,-1]]. What is the top-left entry of A^3?
quiz.explanation: Cube only the diagonal eigenvalues: D^3=diag(27,1). Multiplying P*D^3*P_inverse gives one-half of[[28,26],[26,28]], so the top-left entry is14. Cubing each entry of A separately would not compute a matrix power.

flashcards.back: Av=lambda*v with v!=0. Positive lambda stretches, negative lambda reverses the arrow, zero collapses it. Real eigenvectors need not exist for an arbitrary real matrix.
Eigenvalues sum to the trace $a + d$ and multiply to the determinant $\det A$ - instant cross-checks.
$A = PDP^{-1}$ (columns of P = eigenvectors); $A^k = P D^k P^{-1}$, i.e. just scale each eigendirection k times.

flashcards.front: Why symmetric matrices are special for eigen-analysis
flashcards.back: Real eigenvalues, always diagonalisable, and eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal, which is why covariance PCA gives uncorrelated factors.
[1. 3.], ascending eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix; the eigenvectors are (1, -1) and (1, 1) respectively.
